job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the middle of a master's in software engineering. Mornings I'm in class or working on a group project, a booking system for a dental clinic. Afternoons I work at a phone shop three days a week. I sleep on the sofa in my aunt Marisol's flat in Kestrel Road, with her two kids, because my parents are far away and can't send money. I use an AI coding assistant now and then, mostly when I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, because a lot of the claims were marketing. I'd tell the class that the tools help a bit with boilerplate but don't write real systems. I'd also say it quietly, because the people who said the opposite are the ones who'll interview me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better than the other worlds but my situation is shaky anyway. I've got a heavy loan, almost no savings and a lot of other graduates applying for the same few openings near here. Last year the firm where I interned, Brightpay, let go of five developers in one afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the phone shop job and apply to sixty places, from banks to small agencies. I'd build a portfolio site with my dental booking project. And I'd ask Brightpay's old team lead, Mr Okoro, for a reference, because he liked my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and tired. I like what I study, but I keep thinking about my aunt's sofa and the fact I'm costing her a lot in electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your aunt's flat is crowded. How long can you stay there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another year, maybe, before it gets tense. She'd never say anything, but I can feel it. If I don't land something by next autumn, I'll look at a cheaper town or a call centre job, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the startup do with the other developers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They told them in a meeting at four o'clock and had their laptops back by five. The company said the market had changed. I saw the engineers' faces in the corridor, and that's why I want a boring, stable job.

say: I'd tell the class the tools help a bit with **boilerplate** but don't build real systems.
I'd keep it low-key, because interviewers may hold the **opposite view**.
think: Plateau is better than the others, but my **loan and savings** still make things shaky.
Many graduates chase the same few openings, and **Brightpay** laid off five developers in one afternoon.
do: Apply to **sixty places**, from banks to small agencies.
Build a **portfolio site** using my dental booking project.
Ask Mr Okoro (my old team lead) for a **reference**.
feel: **Uneasy and tired**, guilty about costing my aunt electricity.
S0.quote: I saw the engineers' faces in the corridor, and that's why I want a boring, stable job.
fieldNote: Had a front-row view of **layoffs** at her internship, which shapes her caution.
Guilt about her aunt's household is a constant background.
Centre politics: sceptical of hype and of grand claims.

steps.text: Apply to sixty banks, agencies and small firms
Build a portfolio site from the dental booking project
Keep working three days a week at the phone shop
Ask Mr Okoro at Brightpay for a reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market is going to be tough for new developers, and companies should be honest about it. I'd tell friends to build a record of real work, not just certificates. I wouldn't blame anyone; it's what happens when a tool gets cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my danger zone. Coding is on the list, and entry-level developers are exactly the people who get replaced by a senior with a tool. At Brightpay, a lead started doing the small tickets herself with an assistant, and the junior tickets stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the assistant on purpose and get good at it, so I'm the junior who can use it well. I'd target jobs that mix coding with something else, like banking operations or healthcare systems. And I'd save part of my phone shop pay for a deposit on a room, because I need to leave my aunt's by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, like waiting for an exam result that decides everything. I'd keep my face calm at the phone shop and then go home and refresh the job board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Coding is on the card by name. How much of your own training is this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All of it. Junior tickets, test writing, the small bug fixes. Those were what the interns did, and now they're what a tool does. That's my first-year work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Marisol's flat if the job search stretches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a friend for a spare room and keep working the shop. Failing that, I'd go back to my parents, which would mean giving up on the field. I don't want to, but I'd rather be honest about the option.

say: I'd tell friends to build a **record of real work**, not just certificates.
I'd say companies should be **honest** about hiring fewer juniors.
think: Entry-level developers are exactly who a **senior with a tool** replaces.
The small tickets I'd learn on are **disappearing**, and my first year depends on them.
do: Learn the AI assistant **properly** so I'm the junior who uses it well.
Target jobs that mix coding with **banking or healthcare** systems.
Save part of my phone shop pay for a **room deposit** by spring.
feel: **Anxious**, like waiting on an exam result that decides everything.
S1.quote: Entry-level developers are exactly the people who get replaced by a senior with a tool.
fieldNote: Her field is the **sharpest exposed**: junior coding tickets are already shrinking.
Plans to get good with the tools and mix coding with another field.
Honest that going home may mean leaving the field.

steps.text: Learn the AI coding assistant properly through weekly projects
Apply for jobs that mix coding with banking or healthcare systems
Save part of my phone shop pay for a room deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and look after people, and I'd be one of those quietly telling friends to save. I wouldn't go on marches, but I'd sign whatever helps. I'd also say don't rely on any one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in trouble. By 2028 AI does almost any thinking work, and software development is the first on the list. I'd graduate into the hole, with a loan and a sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop looking only at developer jobs and apply to anything that pays, including logistics and the phone shop full-time. I'd keep my AI skills sharp in case there's a niche. And I'd ask Marisol if I can stay a few more months while I save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd probably wake at four in the morning counting. Then I'd get up and make breakfast for her kids, because that's the thing I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years leaves you graduating into this. What's the first thing you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, yes. They'd worry and tell me to come home. But I'd say I need to try here first, and my mother would send me food in the post, which is how she says it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is full-time at the shop the first plan? Probably the second plan. The first is anything with a pay cheque that uses my degree. The second is the shop, with the third being home.

say: I'd say we need to **slow down** and look after people, and not rely on one employer.
I'd sign **whatever helps**, though I wouldn't march.
think: Software development is the **first on the list**, and I'd graduate into the hole.
I'd have a **loan and a sofa** and not much else.
do: Apply for **any job** that pays, including logistics and full-time at the shop.
Keep my **AI skills** sharp in case a niche appears.
Ask **Marisol** (my aunt) if I can stay a few more months.
feel: **Alarmed**, waking at four in the morning to count money.
S2.quote: I'd graduate into the hole, with a loan and a sofa.
fieldNote: Software is the field named in the card, so the effect on her is **direct**.
Plans fall back through the phone shop, then going home.
Her coping is practical: she makes breakfast for her cousins.

steps.text: Apply for any paid job, including logistics and full-time at the shop
Keep practising with AI coding tools in case a niche appears
Ask my aunt to let me stay a few more months to save
Cut every cost except transport and the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain, if governments and firms pay for it. I'd tell friends to keep learning and to avoid debts they can't carry. I'd say it without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel a bit better but it's still bad. By 2031 I might have two years of work if I get lucky, but entry-level coding is the first to go. I'd know it was coming, which is better than being surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find any junior job in a company that uses software heavily, even outside tech, and learn the business as well as the code. I'd save a third of every cheque and move out of my aunt's flat. I'd also take a certification in cloud security, because it might need people longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but the kind that makes me plan rather than freeze. Like watching a bus come and knowing the stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Do you feel any safer, or just later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Later, I think, and a bit safer. Later gives me a start. I'd use the first two years to get a job, build a savings pot of three months and learn how an industry works, not just a language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first two of those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cybersecurity, maybe, or systems for a hospital. Somewhere where a person has to check what the machine does and answer if it's wrong. I'd be the one who answers.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **retrain** if governments and firms pay for it.
I'd tell friends to **avoid debts** they can't carry.
think: I feel a bit better, but entry-level coding is still the **first to go**.
Knowing it's coming is better than being **surprised**.
do: Find a **junior job** in a software-heavy company, even outside tech, and learn the business.
Save a third of each cheque and **move out** of my aunt's flat.
feel: **Alarmed**, but in a way that makes me plan rather than freeze.
S3.quote: Somewhere where a person has to check what the machine does and answer if it's wrong. I'd be the one who answers.
fieldNote: Time lets her turn fear into **targets**: security, hospitals, accountability roles.
Still alarmed because the entry gate to her field narrows first.
Wants to be the person responsible, a human check.

steps.text: Find a junior job in a software-heavy firm outside tech
Save a third of each cheque and move out of my aunt's flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone time to adjust, if they use it. I'd tell people to pick a skill that deals with people and risk, because those last. I'd stay out of the argument about who's to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel okay. I'd have a decade of work in front of me, a smaller loan and a field that's changing but has places for people who can check and fix. It's still a worry, but it's a normal one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, take a decent job, pay the loan within six years and move into my own place. I'd retrain every two years, say, in security or data. I'd bring my parents over if I could, or at least fly them in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than anywhere else, but not calm. I'd still keep a rainy day fund, because I've seen how a bad afternoon looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What do you look forward to in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a flat big enough for my parents to visit, and to pay back my aunt Marisol, who put up with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it all happens at once. If the firms wait and then rush, the ten years don't help. I'd want a rule that tells them to hire and train graduates along the way.

say: I'd tell people to pick skills that deal with **people and risk**, because they last.
I'd avoid the argument about **who's to blame**.
think: A decade of work, a smaller loan and a field with space for people who can **check and fix**.
It's a worry, but a **normal** one.
do: Pay off the loan within **six years** and move into my own place.
**Retrain** every two years, in security or data.
Bring my **parents** over or at least fly them in.
feel: **Calmer** than anywhere else, but I'd keep a rainy day fund.
S4.quote: I'd want a flat big enough for my parents to visit, and to pay back my aunt Marisol, who put up with me.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, a first job and **debt** keep her in the anxious range.
Her goals are about family: parents and aunt.
Fear is of firms that wait and then rush.

steps.text: Take a decent job and clear the loan within six years
Retrain in security or data every two years
Rent a flat big enough for my parents to visit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my own field gets hit first and I'd have no time. What would help is a graduate scheme that places people in jobs that need a human check, and money to cover rent while I look.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'm grateful for. My aunt Marisol took me in when she didn't have to, and whatever happens to the job market, I'm paying her back.

headlineQuote: My aunt Marisol took me in when she didn't have to, and whatever happens to the job market, I'm paying her back.
portrait: Aisha is a **24-year-old** top software graduate doing a master's, sleeping on her aunt's sofa and working at a phone shop.
She saw **layoffs** at her internship firm, which makes her wary and quiet about her fears.
She uses an AI coding assistant **now and then** and learns to use it properly when the stakes rise.
Her mood is **alarmed** in the fast-change worlds, because junior coding is the first thing to go.
She wants to be the human who checks the machine, and plans to repay her aunt.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because her own field is hit first and there's no time.
whatWouldHelp: A **graduate placement** scheme in jobs needing human checks, plus rent support while she looks.
